title: The way returns
hook: returning is the movement of the Tao; yielding is its way (Tao Te Ching 40)

segments.voice: Yesterday, rooted in the humble: the high stands on the low, the way a tree stands on what's underground. Your line was rooted low. Did you do one humble task, and did anyone notice? Day one thousand one hundred two.

A swing at a playground goes forward as far as it can, hangs at the top for half a second, and comes back. Nobody calls that a failure. The coming back is how it gets to go forward again. A tide runs out across the sand and then returns. A breath goes out, and the next one comes in. Chapter forty of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it opens on exactly this kind of motion: the way things go out, and the way they come home.
screen: `A SWING GOES OUT AND COMES BACK.` → `A TIDE, A BREATH.` → `CHAPTER FORTY.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. James Legge set the opening as a little verse: "The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds." Legge heard the first idea as contraries: things turning toward their opposites. Other translators render the same opening as returning: the way moves by coming back. Some readers hear both at once. What grows full turns toward empty. What goes out comes home. Second, where it returns to. Chapter sixteen spoke of all things returning to their root, and chapter forty ends on the same note: everything under heaven comes from being, and being comes from non-being. So the return isn't only a swing back and forth. It's a coming home to where things started. Third, the other half of the opening: weakness marks the course. The way doesn't shove. It yields, the way water gives ground and still finds its level. Returning and yielding sit side by side in the chapter, like one motion seen from two angles. Fourth, closer to home. A lot of life is arranged around going out: further, faster, more. Chapter forty quietly suggests that turning back is part of the movement, not a break in it. Coming back to a friend you drifted from. Picking up a book you set down halfway. Returning to a practice after a gap of weeks. In this reading, returning isn't starting over. It's how the way moves.
screen: `CONTRARIES, OR RETURNING.` · `HOME TO THE ROOT.` · `WEAKNESS MARKS THE COURSE.` · `COMING BACK ISN'T STARTING OVER.` · then, large: `THE WAY RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: return to something you left. Sit comfortably and let one thing come to mind that you once did and then set down. A walk you used to take. A person you meant to write to. An instrument in a closet. A prayer, if you pray, or a quiet morning hour, if you don't. Don't scold yourself for the gap. Just turn toward it, the way a breath turns and comes back in. Then let your breathing do the teaching: out, a pause, and back. The bell holds the time.
The way returns. Chapter forty's movement: the Tao goes out and comes back, and it yields as it goes. Today's word.
Your line: returning. Pick one thing you left and come back to it today, even for five minutes, without making a speech about the gap. Day one thousand one hundred two.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty as a picture of the way moving in cycles, and some treat a return to an abandoned practice or relationship as part of that movement rather than a failure.

original.note: Chinese: the opening word of chapter forty, rendered 'contraries' by Legge and 'returning' by other translators.

trapdoor: what you thought: the way returns sounds like going backward.
what it means: the Tao moves by turning back and by yielding, the way a breath goes out and comes in.
what a scholar hears: 反, which Legge renders as contraries and others as returning; the chapter then traces being back to non-being.
